g6-2023-039.quote: Write two sentences that describe a ratio of types of animals
g6-2023-039.why: The item shows a collection of five shapes and asks for the ratio of circles to the total number of shapes. This Cool-down shows a collection of dogs, mice and cats and asks students to write ratio sentences about it - the same read-a-collection-and-name-the-ratio task. Caveat: every ratio IM asks for here is part-to-part; the part-to-whole form the test uses is never asked outright (nearest is Unit 2 Lesson 15, Cubes of Paint).

g6-2025-028.quote: Create categories whose quantities can be rearranged into smaller groups
g6-2025-028.why: The item gives four grade-level counts, asks students to combine them into two categories (12+6 to 2+8) and name the ratio in lowest terms, 9:5, with a reversed 5:9 distractor. This activity has students sort a collection into categories, count them, and write ratio sentences, and its narrative explicitly monitors for regrouping counts into smaller equal groups and for ratios written in the opposite order. The simplification step is formalised later in Lesson 5, Defining Equivalent Ratios.

g6-2026-012.quote: the ratio between the two quantities and their total
g6-2026-012.why: The item gives 12 daisies, 20 roses, 13 tulips and asks for roses to the total; the trap distractor 20:25 is the part-to-part ratio, so the whole item turns on part versus whole. Cubes of Paint is the only grade 6 activity that asks students to relate the two quantities in a ratio to their total (5 ml red and 3 ml blue making 8 ml maroon). No IM activity asks students to write that relationship as a ratio, which is why confidence is only medium.

g6-2026-028.quote: circle all those that correctly describe this situation
g6-2026-028.why: The item states 6 eggs for every 4 cups of flour and asks which 'for every' statement is true, the answer being the regrouped 3 eggs to 2 cups. This activity gives 2 cups white to 6 tablespoons blue and asks students to circle every statement that correctly describes it, with the same distractor family: regrouped statements (1 cup for every 3 tablespoons) and reversed-order statements.

g6-2023-041.quote: Which is the better deal? Explain how you know.
g6-2023-041.why: The item gives two stores selling the same candle in different quantities (6 for $12.00, 8 for $14.00) and asks which sells at the lower unit rate. This Cool-down is the same question with the same structure: two pack sizes of rulers at two prices, decide which is the better deal, which requires computing both prices per one.

g6-2024-031.quote: For each situation, find the unit rates.
g6-2024-031.why: The item gives 104 calories per 8-ounce serving and asks for the calories in 1 ounce. This is the activity where the term unit rate is introduced and where students compute the amount per 1 in a non-price context (10 gallons of detergent every 6 weeks, gallons per week), exactly the division the item requires.

g6-2024-039.quote: students explore two unit rates associated with the ratio
g6-2024-039.why: The item gives a 6 gallons orange to 8 gallons blue ratio and asks how much orange goes with 1 gallon of blue - the unit rate for the harder direction, 0.75. Cooking Kinche is built on exactly that move: from the 6:15 wheat-to-water ratio, students decide whether 0.4 cup of wheat per cup of water and 2.5 cups of water per cup of wheat both describe the recipe, and then use one of them.

g6-2025-035.quote: students compare rates per 1 in a shopping context
g6-2025-035.why: The item gives $6.25 for 5 pounds of oranges and $6.90 for 6 pounds of apples and asks which statement about the two unit prices is true, so both unit prices must be computed and compared. This activity is the shopping-context comparison of prices per 1 across several offers. It asks for the lowest price rather than the greatest, which is the only mismatch.

g6-2026-001.quote: How far did each person move in 1 second?
g6-2026-001.why: The item says sound travels 686 meters in 2 seconds and asks for the speed in meters per second. This activity asks exactly that question of runners' data (40 meters in 10 seconds), and it is the lesson where 'meters per second' enters the course.

g6-2026-044.quote: A store sells wooden rulers in packs of 10 and packs of 6.
g6-2026-044.why: The item gives 6 rolls for $12.24 and 9 rolls for $19.62, asks which store has the lower price per roll, and requires the unit rate for each store in the answer. This Cool-down is the same task with equally unfriendly numbers ($8.49 for 10, $5.40 for 6): two pack sizes, compute both prices per one, say which is better.

g6-2023-032.quote: Complete the table so that ratios represented by each row are equivalent
g6-2023-032.why: The item shows a teachers-to-students table with three cells missing and asks which completed table keeps the ratio constant. This activity gives students a partly filled table of a 7:5 recipe and asks them to complete it so that every row is an equivalent ratio, with values deliberately out of order so that skip counting will not work - the same reasoning the item's distractors punish.

g6-2024-046.lessonTitle: Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates
g6-2024-046.quote: Complete the table to show the cost for 4 binders and 10 binders
g6-2024-046.why: The item gives two savings tables (Rex $18 per 2 months, Nero $36 per 3 months) and asks for the difference in savings at 16 months, a row past the end of both tables. This activity has students extend a cost table to new row values and add a unit-price column, establishing that the unit rate is the factor that carries one column to the other - which is how a student gets from 2 months to 16.

g6-2025-001.activity: Batches of Cookies in a Table
g6-2025-001.quote: Write a sentence that describes a ratio shown in the table
g6-2025-001.why: The item asks which of four tables represents a 2 cups cheese to 8 ounces noodles recipe; the wrong tables add a fixed amount down the rows instead of scaling. This Cool-down puts a recipe table in front of students and asks them to state the ratio it shows and to add another equivalent row, which is the same read-the-table-as-equivalent-ratios judgement. IM never poses it as a choose-the-right-table question, so confidence is medium.

g6-2026-010.quote: What point on the graph would represent the time it takes
g6-2026-010.why: The item plots (2,18), (4,36), (6,54) for a hose filling a pool and asks how many gallons at 3 minutes - a point that is not plotted. This Cool-down asks students what a given point on a constant-rate graph means and what point would represent a value not shown, which is the same graph-reading-plus-unit-rate move. Unit 6 Lesson 16, Painting the Set, is where such ratio pairs are first plotted.

g6-2026-034.lessonTitle: Tables and Double Number Line Diagrams
g6-2026-034.quote: Do you agree that this table represents the situation?
g6-2026-034.why: The item says 3 notebooks cost $6 and asks which table shows that relationship; the distractors swap which row holds the counts and which holds the prices, or double the wrong quantity. This Warm-up hands students a table that conflicts with the situation described (the headerless table puts 3,000 in the wrong place) and asks whether it really represents the situation - the same attention to which quantity sits where.

g6-2023-034.quote: when a quantity is measured in two different units, the two measurements form a ratio
g6-2023-034.why: The item gives the ratio 3,520 yards to 2 miles and asks for the yards in 5 miles. Road Sign is built on the same idea - 8 kilometers is about 5 miles, so find the amount for 1 mile and then use it - which is the yards-per-mile route the item wants. The item is a bare scaling with no context beyond the units, so the fit is good but not exact.

g6-2023-036.lessonTitle: Tables and Double Number Line Diagrams
g6-2023-036.quote: At this rate, how long would it take her to bike 3,000 meters?
g6-2023-036.why: The item says Mark ran 8 miles in 60 minutes and asks how long 12 miles takes at that rate. This activity asks the identical question of a cyclist (150 meters in 20 seconds, how long for 3,000 meters) and expects students to build a table of equivalent ratios to get there.

g6-2023-044.lessonTitle: Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates
g6-2023-044.quote: Complete the table to represent a cheetah running at a constant speed
g6-2023-044.why: The item gives two time-and-distance tables for cars at constant speed and asks for the difference in distance at 8 hours. This Cool-down is the same table: time, distance and a speed column at a constant rate, with students filling in a distance for a time that is not listed. The item only adds a subtraction at the end.

g6-2024-034.quote: At this rate, how long will it take this crew to wash
g6-2024-034.why: The item says a machine makes 7 pounds of chocolate in 42 minutes and asks how long 9 pounds takes. This activity asks exactly that shape of question - 15 windows in 18 minutes, how long for a number of windows that is not a multiple of 15 - and its narrative walks through finding the time for one unit and scaling.

g6-2025-016.quote: more efficient ways to compare speeds, namely, by computing rates per 1
g6-2025-016.why: The item gives Copier A 350 pages in 7 minutes and Copier B 210 pages in 3 minutes and asks how many more pages per minute B prints, so both rates per 1 must be found and then subtracted. This activity is where students learn to compare two rates by computing per-1 values. The subtraction step is asked only in the optional Lesson 9 activity Swimming and Biking ('How much faster is that person than the other?'), which is the closer match but sits in a lesson the pacing table marks optional.

g6-2025-045.lessonTitle: Navigating a Table of Equivalent Ratios
g6-2025-045.quote: finding an equivalent ratio where one of the quantities is 1
g6-2025-045.why: The item gives a 2 cups sesame to 5 cups pretzels ratio and asks for the pretzels that go with 3 cups of sesame - a non-integer answer, 7.5, because 3 is not a multiple of 2. This activity is the one that teaches that exact move: when the quantities are not multiples of each other (5 hours and 8 hours of pay), go through the value for 1 first.

g6-2026-021.quote: Find the number of windows that can be washed in 1 minute
g6-2026-021.why: The item says Tina makes 6 decorations in 39 minutes and asks how long 14 take, which forces a non-integer rate of 6.5 minutes each. This activity is the same question with numbers deliberately chosen so the target is not a multiple of the given ratio, and its narrative names finding the amount for 1 and scaling as the way through.

g6-2023-031.why: The item asks, bare of context, '60 is 75% of what number?'. This activity asks the identical question in the identical form - 9 is 50%, 25%, 10% and then 75% of what number - and expects it done mentally from benchmark percentages.

g6-2024-033.quote: students find the values that correspond to 100% when different benchmark percentages are known
g6-2024-033.why: The item asks '4 is 16% of what number?'. This activity asks that question form directly, but only for benchmark percentages (50%, 25%, 10%, 75%). Sixteen percent is not a benchmark, so the item needs a route through 1% that grade 6 only ever practises in the forward direction (Lesson 15, Some Percentage for Charity). Nothing in the course asks students to find 100% from a non-benchmark percentage other than the 30% question in Lesson 11, Puppies Grow Up.

g6-2025-021.quote: What percentage of the school population is that?
g6-2025-021.why: The item gives a table of 50 students' hobby votes and asks what percent chose either of two hobbies (12+11 of 50, so 46%). This Cool-down is the same question with the same numbers - 23 of a school of 50 - and asks for the percentage. It sits in Lesson 16, which the pacing table marks optional; the required runner-up is the Lesson 14 Warm-up, Matching the Percentage, which asks 'B is what percentage of C' but only for benchmark-friendly pairs.

g6-2025-037.quote: This is 75% of the water that a large tank holds
g6-2025-037.why: The item says 6 students are 24% of a class and asks for the class size. This Cool-down is the same find-the-whole question in context (36 liters is 75% of a large tank, how much does the tank hold). The item's 24% is not a benchmark percentage, so the arithmetic route is harder than anything this Cool-down asks; the nearest non-benchmark example in the course is the 30% question in Lesson 11, Puppies Grow Up.

g6-2026-024.lessonTitle: Representing Percentages with Double Number Line Diagrams
g6-2026-024.why: The item says a player scored 6 goals, 30% of the team's total, and asks for the total. This activity asks students to find 100% of a quantity given 20% and then given 30% - the second question is literally this item, and its narrative discusses why 30% is the awkward one because 100 is not a multiple of 30.

g6-2026-031.quote: students determine what percentage one number is of another number
g6-2026-031.why: The item gives an art-club survey table (18, 21, 11) and asks what percent chose vanilla, so students must total the table to 50 first and then find 21 of 50. This Warm-up asks the 'B is what percentage of C' question directly and is in a required lesson. The closer match, Restaurant Capacity in Lesson 16 ('What percentage of its capacity is 9 people?'), is in the lesson the pacing table marks optional.

g6-2024-023.why: The item asks how many pints are in 6 gallons. This Cool-down hands students the same conversion fact - 8 pints in 1 gallon - and makes them convert 5 gallons to pints to compare two buckets.

g6-2025-032.quote: The speed limit on a Canadian highway is 80 kilometers per hour
g6-2025-032.why: The item gives 12 miles per hour and asks for feet per minute, which needs two conversions at once (miles to feet, hours to minutes). Road Sign is the only place in grade 6 where a speed expressed in one pair of units has to be re-expressed in another (80 kilometers per hour against 75 miles per hour), but it converts only the distance unit, so the item asks for a step more than the curriculum does.

g6-2026-003.quote: Students will need to decide whether to multiply or divide by the unit rate
g6-2026-003.why: The item asks which expression converts 72 ounces to pounds, with the four choices being 72 divided by, times, minus and plus 16 - so the whole item is the choice of operation. That is exactly what this activity's narrative names as the demand, and the activity makes students convert in both directions with the 1-to-16 conversion factor.

g6-2026-015.quote: it says that 1 cup equals 16 tablespoons
g6-2026-015.why: The item says Marty has only a tablespoon and knows 1 cup is 16 tablespoons, and asks how many tablespoons make 3/4 cup. This activity is the same situation down to the conversion factor - Diego has only a tablespoon, the cookbook says 1 cup equals 16 tablespoons - and its first question asks for 1/4 cup of almonds in tablespoons.
